system: Behavioral Health, Nervous Systems and Special Senses
outline: Traumatic and mechanical disorders and disorders of increased intracranial pressure
primary_competency: Patient Care: Diagnosis, including history and physical examination
mechanism: Idiopathic intracranial hypertension is a syndrome of increased intracranial pressure without an intracranial mass, hydrocephalus, venous sinus thrombosis, or other identified structural cause. It commonly presents with headache, papilledema, transient visual symptoms, pulsatile tinnitus, and sometimes sixth-nerve palsy. Diagnosis requires exclusion of secondary causes with neuroimaging and demonstration of elevated cerebrospinal-fluid opening pressure with otherwise normal CSF composition.
vignette: A 29-year-old woman has 6 weeks of progressively frequent headaches, brief episodes of dimming vision when she bends over, and a rhythmic whooshing sound in both ears that matches her pulse. BMI is 36 kg/m². Funduscopic examination shows bilateral optic-disc swelling. Neurologic examination is otherwise normal. MRI of the brain and MR venography show no mass, hydrocephalus, or venous sinus thrombosis. Lumbar puncture shows markedly elevated opening pressure with normal cerebrospinal-fluid composition.
lead: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
distractor_notes: Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis can produce headache, papilledema, visual symptoms, and elevated intracranial pressure. However, MR venography is specifically used to detect venous sinus thrombosis, and the normal MR venogram in this vignette argues against that secondary cause.
Migraine with aura can cause headache and transient visual phenomena, but it does not explain bilateral papilledema and objectively elevated CSF opening pressure.

Optic neuritis typically causes acute loss of vision in one eye, impaired color vision, and pain with eye movement. It does not cause a syndrome of generalized intracranial hypertension with bilateral papilledema and pulsatile tinnitus.

Normal-pressure hydrocephalus classically causes a gait disorder, cognitive impairment, and urinary symptoms with ventricular enlargement. This patient instead has papilledema, pulsatile tinnitus, elevated opening pressure, and no hydrocephalus on imaging.
key_expl: This patient has idiopathic intracranial hypertension. MedlinePlus describes IIH as increased intracranial pressure without an identified intracranial mass and lists headache, visual symptoms, pulsatile tinnitus, papilledema, and possible sixth-nerve palsy among its manifestations. The diagnosis is supported here by bilateral papilledema, transient visual obscurations, pulse-synchronous tinnitus, a normal MRI/MR venogram excluding mass and venous thrombosis, normal CSF composition, and an elevated opening pressure.
objective: Recognize idiopathic intracranial hypertension when headache and visual symptoms occur with papilledema and elevated CSF opening pressure after imaging excludes a mass, hydrocephalus, and cerebral venous sinus thrombosis.

sources.title: Idiopathic intracranial hypertension: MedlinePlus Medical Encyclopedia
sources.support: MedlinePlus describes headache, visual symptoms, tinnitus, papilledema, sixth-nerve palsy, MRI/MR venography, and lumbar puncture as key features/evaluation components of IIH.

sources.title: Intracranial Hypertension
sources.support: NCBI describes papilledema, visual symptoms, neuroimaging to exclude a mass or secondary cause, and lumbar puncture measurement of opening pressure in the evaluation of intracranial hypertension.

sources.title: Cerebral Venous Sinus Thrombosis
sources.support: NCBI describes headache, papilledema, and visual symptoms as possible manifestations of cerebral venous sinus thrombosis and identifies CT or MR venography as confirmatory imaging.

sources.title: Optic neuritis: MedlinePlus Medical Encyclopedia
sources.support: MedlinePlus describes optic neuritis as acute visual loss, often in one eye, with impaired color vision and pain during eye movement.

sources.title: Migraine: MedlinePlus Medical Encyclopedia
sources.support: MedlinePlus describes migraine aura as transient neurologic symptoms, commonly visual phenomena such as blind spots, flashing lights, or zigzag lines.
